title: India Is About to Take 120 Deep-Tech Startups to France. It Is the Country's Biggest Bet Yet on Being More Than a Software Outsourcer.
excerpt: Bharat Innovates 2026, announced by Modi during the India-France Year of Innovation, will showcase semiconductor, satellite, and biotech ventures to global investors in Nice from June 14 to 16.
body:
From June 14 to 16, India will present 120 of its most research-intensive startups to international investors, policymakers, and technology partners at Bharat Innovates 2026 in Nice, France. It is the country's most ambitious attempt yet to redefine its global image — not as the world's back office for software services, but as a builder of frontier hardware, semiconductors, biotech, and space technology.

The event, organized by the Ministry of Education as part of the India-France Year of Innovation, was first announced by Prime Minister Narendra Modi on February 17. The cohort was selected through a national process that began with over 3,000 applications and was narrowed to 137 at a pre-summit at IIT Bombay in March, then further refined to the final 120.

## Why Deep Tech Needs a Different Platform

The startups heading to Nice are not consumer apps or SaaS dashboards. They work on semiconductor design, satellite payloads, synthetic biology, quantum security, AI for drug discovery, clean energy storage, and advanced materials. These are ventures where the gap between a prototype and a commercial product can span years — and where the kind of patient, long-term capital they need is fundamentally different from what funds a food delivery app.

India's traditional venture capital ecosystem, built around quick-flip consumer internet bets, has not served these founders well. Bharat Innovates is designed to bridge that gap by placing deep-tech ventures directly in front of the kind of investors and industrial partners — European defence primes, pharmaceutical conglomerates, aerospace manufacturers — who think in decade-long cycles.

## The Scale of the Ambition

The programme has drawn 180 registrations from 15 countries, including more than 55 CXO-level participants from 10 countries and 45 international investors. The Confederation of Indian Industry is a co-organizer, and the event will feature structured pitch sessions, technology exhibitions, and bilateral matchmaking between Indian founders and European partners.

Prof. Ajay Kumar Sood, the Principal Scientific Adviser to the Government of India, inaugurated the pre-summit at IIT Bombay and emphasized the link between academic research ecosystems and commercial deep-tech ventures. "India's deep-tech innovation is directly connected to its research institutions," he said. "The IITs, IISc, and national laboratories are not just producing talent — they are producing companies."

## India's Innovation Ecosystem by the Numbers

India now has over 200,000 recognized startups and more than 120 unicorns. But the more consequential story is happening beneath the unicorn headlines. A wave of manufacturing-focused startups is forming across multiple layers simultaneously — StrainX in synthetic biology ($13 million raised), Tiea Connectors in semiconductor interconnects (₹77 crore), C2i Semiconductors in AI data centre power ($16.7 million), and Pramatra Space in quantum security components.

At the same time, India's startup profitability wave has accelerated. Cashfree became EBITDA-profitable with ₹1,000 crore in revenue, Pepperfry posted its first profitable quarter, and PhysicsWallah's revenue grew 50 per cent to ₹919 crore. The narrative is shifting from growth-at-all-costs to sustainable, deep-technology ventures that can compete globally.

## The Diaspora Dimension

For the millions of Indian-origin engineers, scientists, and entrepreneurs working in Silicon Valley, London, Paris, and Singapore, Bharat Innovates represents something more than a trade show. It is an invitation to reconnect with India's technology ecosystem as investors, advisors, or co-founders — at a moment when the country's capabilities in semiconductors, space, and biotech have caught up with its ambitions.

The India-France partnership adds diplomatic weight. The bilateral relationship, elevated to a Special Strategic Partnership under Modi and President Macron, now spans defence, civil nuclear energy, climate, space, and digital technology. Innovation is the newest pillar, and arguably the one with the most commercial potential.

The 120 ventures heading to Nice in two weeks carry a simple argument: India builds things now. Not just code. Things.

*Sources: YourStory, Press Information Bureau (Government of India), Confederation of Indian Industry, IIT Bombay*
